title: Boss: the on-call shift
summary: Kill a whole process tree, filter a journal export with jq, and move cron schedules to systemd timers.

steps.title: Pager duty
body: Pager duty. Three tickets are waiting, each on a real machine: a batch job that will not die, an overnight crash to
read out of a journal export, and a set of cron schedules to move to systemd timers.

steps.title: Kill the whole tree
prompt: Page: *"the nightly batch is stuck, kill it"*. `batch-runner` started three `batch-child` processes, and each of those
started two `sleep` processes. Killing only the parent leaves the children running as orphans.
Stop **the whole batch tree** (parent, children and grandchildren). Leave `batch-ui`, an unrelated program, running.
`ps -eo pid,ppid,pgid,sid,cmd --forest` or `pstree -p` shows how they hang together.

checks.name: nothing from the batch job is left
checks.cmd: g=$(cat /opt/dojo/state/batch-pid); for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do pgrep -g "$g" >/dev/null || exit 0; sleep 0.5; done; pgrep -a -g "$g"; exit 1
checks.fail: Some processes of the batch job are still running (listed below). Killing the parent does not kill its children: signal the whole process group.

checks.name: batch-ui still runs
checks.fail: `batch-ui` was stopped too. It is in another process group; leave it alone.

hints: `ps -eo pid,ppid,pgid,cmd --forest` shows the tree. All the batch processes share one **PGID**: the PID of `batch-runner`, which started a new session.
A negative PID means "the whole process group": `kill -TERM -- -PGID`. `pkill -g PGID` does the same.
`kill -TERM -- -$(pgrep -x batch-runner)`, then check with `pgrep -a batch; pgrep -a sleep`.
explain: Process groups exist for exactly this: a shell puts each pipeline or job in its own group, so Ctrl+C reaches every
process in it. `kill -- -PGID` does the same from outside. systemd goes further: each service runs in its own
**cgroup**, so `systemctl stop` finds every process of the service even if one escaped into a new group.

steps.title: Filter the journal with jq
prompt: The on-call notes say orders-api fell over overnight. You got the journal exported with `journalctl -o json`
into `~/incident/journal.json`: one JSON object per line, with fields like `_SYSTEMD_UNIT`, `PRIORITY` and
`MESSAGE`. Every value is a **string**; priorities go from `"0"` (emerg) to `"7"` (debug), `"3"` is err.
1. `~/answers/errors.txt`: the `MESSAGE` of every `orders-api.service` entry with priority **err or worse**, in
order, one per line (what `journalctl -u orders-api -p err -o cat` would print).
2. `~/answers/units.txt`: for **all** units, how many entries of priority err or worse each has, as `count unit`
lines, biggest first (`sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` gives this shape).

checks.name: errors.txt holds the orders-api errors
checks.fail: The messages do not match. Filter on both the unit and the priority, and remember `PRIORITY` is a string: `(.PRIORITY | tonumber) <= 3`. `jq -r` prints raw text without quotes.

checks.name: units.txt counts errors per unit
checks.cmd: diff <(awk '{print $1, $2}' ~/answers/units.txt 2>/dev/null) <(jq -r 'select((.PRIORITY | tonumber) <= 3) | ._SYSTEMD_UNIT' ~/incident/journal.json | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | awk '{print $1, $2}')
checks.fail: The counts do not match. Select err-or-worse entries, print `._SYSTEMD_UNIT`, then `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`.

hints: `head -n2 ~/incident/journal.json | jq .` shows the fields. `jq -r '.MESSAGE'` prints one message per line.
`select(...)` keeps only matching objects: `jq -r 'select(._SYSTEMD_UNIT == "orders-api.service") | .MESSAGE'`. Comparing the string `"3"` with a number does not work as you hope; use `tonumber`.
explain: On the server itself this is `journalctl -u orders-api -p err --since "-12h" -o cat`. The JSON output is for
everything else: shipping logs, counting per unit, or picking fields `journalctl` has no flag for. `-p err` means
"err and more severe", which is why the numbers go **down** as severity goes up.

steps.title: Move cron schedules to timers
prompt: The team is moving jobs from cron to systemd timers. Write the `OnCalendar=` value for each cron schedule into
`~/answers/calendar.txt`, **one per line, in this order** (just the value, without `OnCalendar=`):
1. `0 */6 * * *`: every six hours, on the hour.
3. `0 9 1 * *`: 09:00 on the first day of every month.
`systemd-analyze calendar 'EXPR'` prints how systemd reads an expression and when it fires next. It is the checker: a
line passes when systemd normalises it to the same schedule as the cron line.

checks.name: line 1 means "0 */6 * * *"
checks.cmd: want="*-*-* 00/6:00:00"; got="$(sed -n '1p' ~/answers/calendar.txt 2>/dev/null)"; test -n "$got" && test "$(systemd-analyze calendar "$got" 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^Normalized form: //p')" = "$want"
checks.fail: Line 1 of `~/answers/calendar.txt` does not normalise to `*-*-* 00/6:00:00`. Run `systemd-analyze calendar` on it.

checks.name: line 2 means "*/15 * * * *"
checks.cmd: want="*-*-* *:00/15:00"; got="$(sed -n '2p' ~/answers/calendar.txt 2>/dev/null)"; test -n "$got" && test "$(systemd-analyze calendar "$got" 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^Normalized form: //p')" = "$want"
checks.fail: Line 2 of `~/answers/calendar.txt` does not normalise to `*-*-* *:00/15:00`. Run `systemd-analyze calendar` on it.

checks.name: line 3 means "0 9 1 * *"
checks.cmd: want="*-*-01 09:00:00"; got="$(sed -n '3p' ~/answers/calendar.txt 2>/dev/null)"; test -n "$got" && test "$(systemd-analyze calendar "$got" 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^Normalized form: //p')" = "$want"
checks.fail: Line 3 of `~/answers/calendar.txt` does not normalise to `*-*-01 09:00:00`. Run `systemd-analyze calendar` on it.

checks.name: line 4 means "30 2 * * 1-5"
checks.cmd: want="Mon..Fri *-*-* 02:30:00"; got="$(sed -n '4p' ~/answers/calendar.txt 2>/dev/null)"; test -n "$got" && test "$(systemd-analyze calendar "$got" 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^Normalized form: //p')" = "$want"
checks.fail: Line 4 of `~/answers/calendar.txt` does not normalise to `Mon..Fri *-*-* 02:30:00`. Run `systemd-analyze calendar` on it.

hints: The format is `DayOfWeek Year-Month-Day Hour:Minute:Second`, and `*` means any. `a/b` means "from a, every b": `00/6` in the hour field is 0, 6, 12, 18.
Every 15 minutes is `*:0/15`. The first of the month at nine is `*-*-01 09:00`.
solution: while read -r e; do systemd-analyze calendar "$e" | head -n3; done < ~/answers/calendar.txt
explain: `systemd-analyze calendar --iterations=5 EXPR` lists the next five runs: the fastest way to answer "when does the
backup run next?" without doing calendar maths in your head. For a timer that already exists, `systemctl
list-timers` shows the next and last run of every timer on the machine.
